topic.title: Object-Oriented Programming
topic.description: Classes, inheritance, polymorphism, and object lifecycle.

questions.title: Virtual Functions
questions.explanation: Because `print` is declared virtual in the Base class, the call is resolved dynamically at runtime. Since the actual object is of type Derived, `Derived::print()` is called.

questions.title: Constructor & Destructor Order
questions.explanation: Constructors are called from base to derived (A then B). Destructors are called in the reverse order (B then A).

questions.title: Object Slicing
questions.explanation: The function `display` takes the object by value, causing object slicing. The `Derived` part of `d` is sliced off, and a pure `Base` object is created. Thus, `Base::show()` is called.

questions.title: Static Member Variables
questions.explanation: Static member variables are shared across all instances of a class. The constructor increments it twice.

questions.title: Virtual Destructor
questions.explanation: Because the base class destructor is NOT virtual, deleting a derived object through a base pointer results in undefined behavior, usually only calling the Base destructor.

questions.title: Const Member Functions
questions.explanation: t1 is const, so it calls the const version of getValue (returns 5). t2 is non-const, so it prefers the non-const version (returns 10).

questions.title: Initialization Lists
questions.explanation: Members are initialized in the order they are declared in the class (x then y). x is initialized with y (which is currently garbage), and then y is initialized with a (5). Output is undefined for x.

questions.title: Friend Functions
questions.explanation: Friend functions are not member functions, but they have access to private and protected members of the class.

questions.title: Default Arguments in Virtual Functions
questions.explanation: Default arguments are bound at compile-time based on the pointer type (Base, so x=10). But the function called is bound dynamically (Derived). Hence D10.

questions.title: Pure Virtual Functions
questions.explanation: Concrete provides an implementation for the pure virtual function, allowing it to be instantiated and called via the abstract base pointer.

questions.title: Operator Overloading
questions.explanation: The + operator is overloaded to return a new Point with the sum of the x values.

questions.title: Private Inheritance
questions.explanation: B inherits privately from A, so A's public members become private in B. However, B's own member functions (like bar) can still call them.

questions.title: Delete this
questions.explanation: Deleting `this` is legal as long as the object was allocated on the heap, and you don't access any member variables after deletion. The function continues and prints D.

questions.title: Copy Constructor
questions.explanation: b1 calls the default constructor (C). b2 is initialized with b1, which calls the copy constructor (K).

questions.title: Virtual Inheritance
questions.explanation: Because B and C inherit virtually from A, there is only one shared sub-object A in D. Therefore, A is constructed only once.

questions.title: Mutable Keyword
questions.explanation: The 'mutable' keyword allows a member variable to be modified even if the object is instantiated as 'const' or accessed through a 'const' member function.

questions.title: Private Constructor
questions.explanation: A private constructor prevents direct instantiation. The static member function can still access it to implement the Singleton pattern.

questions.title: Static Method Hiding
questions.explanation: Static methods are not virtual and do not support dynamic dispatch. They are resolved at compile-time based on the static type of the pointer.

questions.title: Object Slicing with Arrays
questions.explanation: Treating an array of derived objects as an array of base objects using pointer arithmetic leads to Undefined Behavior because sizeof(B) is likely greater than sizeof(A). The pointer aPtr[1] calculates the offset using sizeof(A), landing in the middle of a B object.

questions.title: Virtual Destructor and Memory
questions.explanation: Because the base destructor is virtual, deleting a derived object through a base pointer correctly invokes the derived destructor first (count=1), then the base destructor (count=2).
